posts.title: Woodbridge trench collapse: director jailed after excavation undermined a conservatory

body.p: On 15 December 2020 Dale Baker, 30, was working as a labourer on a house renovation at Haughgate Close, Woodbridge. A trench was dug along the side of an existing conservatory as part of extension works. The trench face collapsed onto him and the conservatory foundations followed. A post-mortem recorded suffocation. Suffolk Police and the Health and Safety Executive investigated jointly. On 15 September 2026 at Ipswich Crown Court, Peter Clifford, 63, former director of Hintonwood East Anglia Ltd, was sentenced to eight years and 10 months imprisonment after pleading guilty to gross negligence manslaughter and two offences under the Health and Safety at Work etc. Act 1974. The company admitted the same HSWA offences. Clifford was banned from acting as a company director for 10 years. BBC News and Suffolk Police reported that shuttering was not implemented or was inadequate, that the trench had been dug dangerously close to the conservatory, and that no action was taken to support its foundations. Judge Samantha Leigh, as reported by the East Anglian Daily Times, stated that it should have been obvious to any reasonable competent person that there was a high risk of collapse with potentially catastrophic outcomes.

This is the second high-profile excavation fatality sentenced in the same week as the Banstead Old Bailey case. The lesson is not that large civils sites are the only problem. Domestic extensions, service repairs and small-works trenches produce the same collapse physics. Two mechanisms were present: unsupported soil faces and undermining of an existing structure. Either can be fatal. Cost pressure from a client who wants the work done cheaply does not transfer the duty. HSE excavations guidance remains the statutory-duty starting point: support or batter the sides before anyone enters, keep spoil and plant back from the edge, and inspect after any change that can affect stability. BS 5975-1:2024 is the management benchmark HSE uses when judging whether temporary works were planned, coordinated and inspected. Standard does not automatically mean low risk. A shallow trench next to an existing foundation is high consequence. Provisional category only - to be confirmed by the TWC and the project temporary works procedure.

body.h: Practical TWC and TWS control points
ul: Register every excavation on the Temporary Works Register, including domestic extensions, drainage repairs and service trenches. Size of contract is not a risk filter.
Write a design brief that covers both face stability and influence on existing foundations, drains, boundary walls and public footways. Undermining is a separate temporary works item.
Do not allow entry until support, trench box, shoring or a designed batter is in place. Shuttering that is planned but not installed is not a control.
Keep spoil, plant and materials away from the edge. Surcharge next to an unsupported face is a foreseeable collapse trigger.
Inspect after each shift, after rainfall and after any deepening or widening. A deeper cut than the brief is a changed design.
Hold a permit to enter / permit to excavate signed by a competent person who has seen the support, not only the RAMS.
If a safe method cannot be found next to an existing structure, stop. The court record in this case is explicit that refusing the work is part of the duty.
Independent check category is provisional only. Adjacent occupied structure, unknown foundation depth and no GI normally point to escalation, not a CAT 0 close-out.
